To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sterol release from a StAR domain involves water penetration into a fractured pocket, destabilization of bound sterol, and its release into solution.
the StARkin domains of Lam/GramD proteins exchange sterols with membranes through a fracture in the sterol-binding pocket that is controlled by the presence of water.
the StARkin protein Lam/GramD2 exchanges sterol with the membrane through a mechanism that requires water molecules to penetrate a fracture in the sterol-binding pocket.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure and function of Lam/GramD proteins.
understanding the mechanisms by which proteins control intracellular cholesterol homeostasis.
the molecular mechanisms underlying sterol egress.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the StARkin domains are involved in the transport of sterols from the ER to the plasma membrane, and that the StAR kin domain has evolved to have a unique mechanism of sterol transport that is dependent on the exchange of water and sterol.
the StARkin domains of GramD1 proteins have a water-assisted mechanism for sterol egress.
Lam proteins are involved in intracellular sterols homeostasis, but how this is done is still not fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we identified a new family of sterol binding proteins, we showed how sterols enter and exit these proteins, and we showed that the proteins play a role in the homeostasis of sterols in yeast cells.
Lam/GramD sterols are a family of ER-resident proteins that bind and exchange sterols with membranes, thereby regulating intracellular sterol trafficking and homeostasis.
Lam/GramD proteins, which contain the first known StARkin domains, are implicated in the intracellular trafficking of sterols.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a protein domain that is designed to bind a small, nonpolar ligand, sterol, can use a fracture in its wall to exchange sterol for water.
water can act as a molecular crowbar to pry sterol from a protein-binding site, a process that could have broad implications in the regulation of intracellular sterol levels.
the StARkin domains of Lam/GramD proteins have a unique mechanism for releasing sterol from their sterol-binding pocket.
